name: Athens

areaKm2.note: Hansen 2006 p. 55: Attika could sustain ~100,000 at a carrying capacity of just over 40 per km2, i.e. ~2,400 km2 of mainland Attika; with Salamis ~2,550 km2 (Hansen & Nielsen Inventory gives c. 2,500 km2; not fetched).

population.note: Hansen 2006 (pp. 55-56, nn. 126, 136-137): 4th-century Attika at 150,000 (21,000 adult male citizens) to 210,000 (31,000 adult male citizens; his preferred model: x3.5 for all citizens, +30,000 metics, free:slave 2:1), with Whitby at 250,000-300,000. For 480 BCE, Patterson's 25,000-30,000 adult male citizens (cited in the Hansen literature; Herodotus 5.97 gives 30,000 c. 500) plus fewer metics and slaves than in the 4th century give ~190,000. Citizens, metics and slaves of Attika incl. Salamis.

urbanization.note: Educated guess: Athens (with Phaleron/Piraeus) held perhaps a quarter to a third of Attika's population in the classical period; 480 likely at the lower end.

activePersonnel.note: Sum of hoplites (8,000), archers (~700), light-armed (~4,000) and fleet crews (~33,500). In 480 Athens mobilised nearly all men of military age (Hansen 2006 p. 10); this is ~25% of population, above the validator's 20% warning by design.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: oldest and youngest year classes left for guard duty; in 480 nearly everyone else was already serving.

supportPersonnel.note: Trireme crews: 170 oarsmen + ~16 deck crew/officers per ship (marines and archers are counted as P roles). Low 180 x 170; mid 180 x 186 (the 20 ships lent to Chalcis were crewed by Chalcidians, Herodotus 8.1); high 200 x 186. Rowers included citizens, metics and slaves (Hansen 2006 pp. 10-16).

mobilizationRatio.note: Hansen 2006 p. 10: in 480 perhaps 90% of the year classes 20-49 (Figueira: up to 55) were called up to man the fleet, metics and slaves included. Males 20-55 are ~half of all males, i.e. ~25% of the population; the ratio of the actual 480 effort to total population is ~0.25.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Herodotus 9.28: 8,000 Athenian hoplites at Plataea (479); ~9,000-10,000 at Marathon (490, later sources). Lazenby 1993 accepts figures of this order. In 480 many served as epibatai (10 per trireme) instead.

quality.note: Bronze hoplite panoply among the era's best heavy infantry (0.75).

training.note: Citizen militia without state drill before the ephebeia (rubric 0.25-0.5).

count.note: Athenian archers fought at Plataea (Herodotus 9.22, 9.60); triremes carried 4 archers each (180 x 4 = 720). Thucydides 2.13.8 gives 1,600 archers for 431 (upper bound).

quality.note: Era-typical bows.

training.note: Part-time citizens and hired archers.

count.note: Educated guess: attendants and light-armed (psiloi). Herodotus 9.29 implies ~1 light-armed per hoplite for non-Spartan contingents at Plataea; most were untrained servants.

quality.note: Stones, javelins, no armour (rubric 0.25).

training.note: Untrained (rubric 0.25).

count.note: Herodotus 8.1: 127 Athenian ships at Artemisium + 20 lent to Chalcis, later 53 more (=200); 8.44: 180 at Salamis. The Themistoklean programme of the 480s provided most of them (Ath. Pol. 22.7, cited by Hansen 2006 p. 16 n. 19). Ship counts are better attested than army sizes.

quality.note: New triremes, among the era's best (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Crews trained since the 483/2 programme; less experienced than Phoenician crews.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75 row: proven commanders (Themistocles, Miltiades' legacy, Aristides), but no staff system; mid 0.7.

cohesion.note: Between national conscript (0.5) and professional unit identity (0.75): tribal regiments, democratic polis identity.

morale.note: Rubric 1.0 (existential defence): Attika evacuated and Athens sacked in 480.

weapons.note: Between anchor 2 and 3: iron and bronze spear/sword, no torsion artillery.

armor.note: Close to anchor 3 (bronze cuirass): bronze/linen hoplite panoply.

fortification.note: Anchor 2 (stone citadel: Acropolis); Piraeus fortification begun 493, city walls rebuilt only in 479.

logistics.note: Anchor 2: wagons and carried rations, no depot system; grain imports by sea.

isr.note: Year anchor (480 BCE): scouting ships and lookouts.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Greece year 1 CE = 1,275, Italy 1,407 (2011 int$). Ober (isbn:069114091X, ch. 4 "Wealthy Hellas") argues classical Greek consumption was well above Roman-era levels, peaking in the 4th century; Athens with Laurion silver and trade above the Greek average.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Warfare was the largest public expense of classical Athens (Pritchard, isbn:029277205X); the 483/2 Laurion windfall paid for ~100-200 triremes.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: silver mining at Laurion, ceramics, shipbuilding and crafts.

foodSurplus.note: Hansen 2006 p. 55 n. 125: Attika in normal years could sustain ~100,000 people, so a population of ~190,000 depended on grain imports; no domestic surplus.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical snapshots. Citizen year class alone ~1,000 for 30,000 adult male citizens (Hansen 2006 p. 35).

roadKm.note: Educated guess: a few engineered routes (Sacred Way to Eleusis ~20 km), otherwise tracks.

majorPorts.note: Phaleron and Piraeus (being fortified from 493; shipsheds for the Themistoklean fleet).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: grain imports for ~90,000 people at ~200 kg/person/year = ~18,000 t a year, carried by a merchant fleet making several voyages a season.

supplyRangeKm.note: Hoplite armies marched with ~3 days' rations x ~20 km a day; by sea the fleet's range was a few days' rowing between beaching places.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.02-0.06 oxen, mules and donkeys per inhabitant x population.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1: familiar terrain and local supply; the city walls did not yet stand in 480 (Athens was evacuated and sacked), so not 1.2.

notes: Snapshot = 480 BCE, the Salamis year. Border "none": historical-basemaps world_bc500 only has a single "Greek city-states" polygon (all of Greece incl. Macedonia, plus Magna Graecia and Massalia as further features), which would overstate Athens' territory ~50-fold. Population convention: Attika incl. Salamis, citizens + metics + slaves; no allies. Population for 480 extrapolated from 4th-century models; every Athenian demographic number is disputed (Hansen's "shotgun method"). Active personnel is ~25% of population (validator warning expected): in 480 nearly every able man, incl. metics and slaves, rowed in the fleet. Fleet crews are supportPersonnel per schema; hoplites serving as marines are counted under infantry_line.

name: People's Republic of China

areaKm2.note: asOf 2024. Surface area 9,562,910 km2; low is land area 9,388,210 km2. Excludes Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau (separate World Bank entries).

population.note: asOf 2025 (World Bank 1,406,585,000; 2024 1,408,975,000 = high). Population is falling (~-0.2%/yr); low allows for 2026 decline. Mainland only; excludes Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan.

activePersonnel.note: IISS Military Balance 2026 p.248-249 as quoted: 2,035,000 active. CIA Factbook 2025: ~2 million (Ground 950,000-1,000,000; Navy 250,000 incl. ~50,000 marines; Air Force 350-400,000; Rocket Force 120,000; other 150-175,000). People's Armed Police (~500,000) excluded.

trainedReserves.note: IISS Military Balance 2026: 510,000 reserves. High is an educated allowance for the militia system (primary militia is much larger but untrained for combat).

supportPersonnel.note: Active 2,035,000 minus infantry P roles (150,000 + 110,000). Navy, Air Force (403,000 per IISS 2026 as quoted on the PLAAF article), Rocket Force, Aerospace/Cyberspace/Information Support and Joint Logistics forces, vehicle crews, artillery, staff.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess by analogy: WWII belligerents reached ~10-17% of population (USSR, Germany); China is held lower because the binding constraint is equipment, training cadres and industrial labour, not manpower; 5% is still ~70 million people.

count.note: Educated guess. Ground Force 960,000 (IISS 2025 as quoted) in 13 group armies; ~55 heavy and medium combined-arms brigades x ~2,500-3,000 mechanized infantry. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Ground_Force)

quality.note: Rubric 0.75 among era best: ZBD-04A/ZBL-08 families, digital C2; below US kit.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: two-year conscripts plus a growing NCO corps; intensive exercises but no combat since 1979.

count.note: Educated guess. Light, mountain and amphibious combined-arms brigades, Airborne Corps (~35,000), PLAN Marine Corps (30,000-55,000 per PLAN article, inconsistent), special operations brigades. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Navy)

quality.note: Rubric 0.75 band.

armor.note: Anchor 9 composite armour with some anchor-10 features (Type 99A, ZTQ-15; APS on few vehicles).

ships.note: Anchor 10 networked fleets largely met: Type 055, catapult carrier Fujian (2025), large USV/UUV programs; nuclear submarines lag (anchor 9).

fortification.note: Anchor 10 layered air defence along the coast, hardened underground facilities, fortified South China Sea islands.

logistics.note: Anchor 9-10: Joint Logistics Support Force, dense rail/road network and civilian RO-RO ferries; limited global sealift/airlift (Y-20 growing) and one overseas base.

communications.note: Anchor 10: BeiDou, Tianlian relay satellites, Information Support Force (2024).

isr.note: Anchor 10: Yaogan and other ISR constellations (hundreds of satellites), long-endurance UAVs, over-the-horizon radar.

air.note: Anchor 10 5th generation: J-20 (300+), J-35 entering service.

cyber.note: Anchor 10 state cyber forces: Cyberspace Force (2024), extensive state-linked operations.

gdpPerCapita.note: asOf 2025. World Bank NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD 25,066.5 (2021 int$) x 0.8005 = 20,066 2011 int$. Range +/-15%.

gdp.note: asOf 2025. World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.KD (constant 2021 int$) 35,258,193,185,781 x 0.8005 (US GDP deflator 2011/2021) = 28,224,183,645,218 2011 int$. Range +/-15% for PPP benchmark uncertainty and the relative-price drift the rebase ignores.

milSpendShare.note: SIPRI via World Bank: 1.72% of GDP in 2025, 1.57% in 2021. High allows for spending outside the official budget (R&D, PAP, procurement) that Western estimates add; educated range. CIA Factbook 1.5% (2024).

industrialShare.note: asOf 2025: industry incl. construction 35.6% of GDP; 38.1% in 2021.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: large domestic production but net importer of soybeans, feed grain and meat; low surplus over subsistence under blockade.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 716,046,014 x share of males aged 15-19 6.337% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 9,075,871. Male population from SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10% for single-year cohort variation.

armor.note: Educated guess: Norinco heavy-vehicle plants; no fetched production figure. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Ground_Force)

aircraft_fighter.note: Educated guess consistent with the J-20 fleet growing from ~50 (2020) to ~300 (mid-2025) per the PLAAF article, i.e. ~50/yr for that type alone, plus J-16, J-10C, J-35. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_active_People%27s_Liberation_Army_Air_Force_aircraft)

drones.note: Educated guess for Group 2+ military UAVs; China is the largest civilian drone producer, which a war economy could convert. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_active_People%27s_Liberation_Army_Air_Force_aircraft)

ships_major.note: Educated guess: PLAN commissions roughly a dozen destroyers/frigates/large amphibs per year in recent years; world's largest shipbuilding capacity. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Navy)

submarines.note: Educated guess (Huludao and Wuhan yards). (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Navy)

missiles.note: Educated guess for TEL launchers per year. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force)

roadKm.note: Chinese 2024 transport statistical bulletin as quoted: 5,490,400 km total, 5,344,700 km paved (mid), 190,700 km expressway.

railKm.note: CIA Factbook: 150,000 km (2021) incl. 40,000 km high-speed (mid). World Bank IS.RRS.TOTL.KM 109,767 km (2021) as low. High allows for 2022-2026 growth (educated).

majorPorts.note: CIA Factbook 2024: 66 ports, 5 large + 9 medium = 14 (low); its classification by harbour size understates China, which has ~25-40 major coastal ports handling hundreds of millions of tonnes (educated guess mid/high).

merchantTonnage.note: asOf 2025: 137,064 thousand DWT under the Chinese flag; high adds Hong Kong register 203,048 thousand DWT (Hong Kong is outside ne:CHN but under PRC sovereignty).

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: mechanized PLA formations sustained by the Joint Logistics Support Force and rail; little experience sustaining operations abroad.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess for horses, mules and donkeys (not from FAO data). Militarily marginal (some pack animals in Tibet border units).

nuclearWarheads.note: FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces (beginning 2026): military stockpile 620 (34 deployed, 586 reserve/non-deployed). Low is the 2025 FAS estimate of ~600 (Rocket Force article). High allows for fast growth (US DoD projects >1,000 by 2030).

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: fortified cities, population support, deep strategic depth; 1.3 for invasions into the Tibetan plateau or Xinjiang (harsh climate, altitude).

notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2025 data with 2026 order of battle. Population convention: mainland China inside ne:CHN; Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan excluded. Climate Cwa is the dominant class of the populated east; the west is BWk/ET. Money in 2011 int$ via derived:ppp-rebase-2011 (+/-15% for PPP uncertainty). Force counts: IISS Military Balance 2025-2026 as quoted on Wikipedia (Ground Force, PLAAF list, personnel list), PLAN article (counts partly unsourced there), Rocket Force table. The US DoD 2025 China Military Power Report PDF returned HTTP 403 and was not used. ships_major = carriers/LHD + destroyers + frigates; ships_minor = corvettes, missile boats, LPD/LST/LSM, MCM; drones = Group 3+ UAVs (grade D). Infantry P-role splits and air_defense batteries are educated guesses. People's Armed Police (~500,000), China Coast Guard and maritime militia excluded. Disputed South China Sea outposts listed under basesAbroad because they lie outside the ne:CHN polygon.

name: French Empire

areaKm2.note: world_1800 France polygon = 543,000 km2 on the sphere (old France). Add annexed departments: Belgium ~30,500, left bank of the Rhine ~25,000, Piedmont ~25,000, Liguria ~5,400, Geneva and Mulhouse small.

population.note: France in modern borders 29.0M (1800) and 30.1M (1810) per HYDE/Gapminder (OWID), interpolated 29.5M for 1805, plus the annexed departments of 1805: Belgium 3.25M (OWID 1800), left bank of the Rhine ~1.6M, Piedmont and Liguria (annexed 1802/June 1805) ~2.3M. Low drops the Italian annexations; high allows for under-counting.

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) urban share for France: 26.3% (1800), 28.2% (1810) = high end. Narrower definitions (towns >5,000) give ~12%. Mid between.

activePersonnel.note: Reconstruction. Grande Armee for the Ulm campaign 210,000 (Chandler, Campaigns of Napoleon p. 384; Clodfelter 2017 p. 152 gives 165,200), Massena's Army of Italy ~50,000, Gouvion St-Cyr in Naples ~20,000, Holland/Hanover, coast and interior garrisons, depots, plus ~60,000 navy. Paper strengths of 90 line and 27 light regiments and 80 cavalry regiments total ~400,000 army.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: reserve portion of the annual conscript classes and depot battalions callable within a month (Elting ch. 9 on the reserve list); national guard untrained.

supportPersonnel.note: Artillery (foot, horse, train) ~30,000, engineers and pontonniers ~5,000, military train and administration ~10,000, staffs, gendarmerie ~15,000, navy and marines ~60,000. Reconstruction from Elting's branch chapters; grade C.

mobilizationRatio.note: Napoleonic conscription raised ~2.0M men 1800-1814 (Bodart, via Elting, Swords Around a Throne ch. 9) from a 30-44M empire; the 1813-14 peak under arms (~1.2M incl. allies, John France 2011 p. 351) is the practical ceiling, ~6-9% of population. 1793-94 levee en masse ~1M of 28M.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: 90 ligne regiments (paper 3 battalions, ~2,500 present) plus Guard grenadiers and chasseurs a pied (Guard ~12,000 total in 1805). Reconstruction from regimental counts; grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75 (among the era's best). Evidence: Charleville 1777 musket, era-standard, with superior organisation

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: Grande Armee corps drilled two years in the Boulogne camps 1803-05 (Chandler pt. 7); veteran cadres from 1792-1801; non-Grande Armee units weaker

count.note: 27 legere regiments at ~2,200 present, plus voltigeur companies already counted in the line. Grade C reconstruction.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: same musket; skirmish tactics the era's best

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: Boulogne training, revolutionary skirmish tradition

count.note: 2 carabinier and 12 cuirassier regiments (~600 present each) plus Guard grenadiers a cheval.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: cuirass reissued 1802-04; good big horses scarce

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: cavalry still rebuilding after the 1790s; d'Hautpoul and Nansouty divisions well drilled

count.note: 30 dragoon (counted here as the schema puts dragoons in light cavalry), 24-26 chasseur and 10 hussar regiments plus Guard chasseurs a cheval; many dragoons were dismounted in 1805.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: horse supply weaker than Austria's; dragoons partly dismounted

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: Murat's reserve cavalry screened the Black Forest effectively (Chandler pt. 7)

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: long-service professional gunners, horse artillery the era's best

count.note: Ships of the line in commission 1805: 18 French at Trafalgar (Villeneuve), 21 with Ganteaume at Brest, 5 with Allemand at Rochefort, plus ships fitting out. Educated reconstruction; grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: French 74s were among the best designs of the era

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: crews blockaded in port, poor gunnery and seamanship versus the Royal Navy

count.note: Frigates and corvettes in service; educated guess.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: good French frigate designs

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: blockade-bound crews

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 1.0 (best-in-era: "Napoleon 1805" is the rubric example). Evidence: Ulm envelopment and Austerlitz; corps system with Davout, Soult, Lannes, Ney (Chandler pt. 7-8)

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75 (professional with strong unit identity). Evidence: veteran regiments after two years together at Boulogne; conscripts a minority in 1805

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75 (motivated, recent victories). Evidence: victories of 1796-1800, new Empire, marshalate

weapons.note: Anchor: 6 (1805: flintlock musket, 12-pdr, Gribeauval). Evidence: the anchor is this army

armor.note: Anchor: 6 (none / cuirass). Evidence: cuirassiers re-armoured 1802-04

ships.note: Anchor: 6 (74-gun ships of the line). Evidence: French 74s set the standard; no steam yet

fortification.note: Anchor: 6 (Vauban-type forts). Evidence: Vauban belt on the north-east frontier, Strasbourg, Metz, Mainz

logistics.note: Anchor: 6 (magazines + requisition). Evidence: living off the land plus forward magazines let the Grande Armee march Boulogne to Danube in ~5 weeks (van Creveld, Supplying War ch. 2)

communications.note: Anchor: 6 (semaphore telegraph). Evidence: Chappe telegraph lines Paris-Strasbourg-Lille-Brest-Lyon in service

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years: 1805 -> 6. Evidence: cavalry screens and spies (Schulmeister) fed Napoleon Mack's position

air.note: Military ballooning (aerostiers) disbanded 1799; no aircraft before 1903.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023, France: 1800 = 1,660, 1805 = 1,892, 1810 = 1,917 (2011 int$). Annexed Belgium and Rhineland were richer, Piedmont poorer; net taken as the French value.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: war and navy took roughly 60% of a state budget of ~700M francs against national income of ~7-8bn francs; 1805 was a war year, so peacetime share is lower.

industrialShare.note: Analogue: industry and crafts ~20-25% of French product c. 1800 in the Toutain/Marczewski national accounts as usually summarised; agriculture ~half. Grade C.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: grain self-sufficient in normal years, ~60% of labour in farming.

annualCohort.note: Males reaching 20 per class: ~1.0-1.1% of a 33-37M population; Napoleon called 60,000-80,000 per class in 1805-06 (Elting ch. 9), the rest exempt, unfit or held in reserve.

artillery.note: Educated guess for field-gun output of the Douai, Strasbourg and other foundries per year.

ships_major.note: Educated guess: ships of the line launched per year 1803-1806 in French and annexed (Antwerp, Genoa) yards.

roadKm.note: Routes imperiales (~30,000-35,000 km, classified 1811) plus maintained departmental roads. Educated reconstruction; grade C.

majorPorts.note: Brest, Toulon, Rochefort, Lorient, Cherbourg, Antwerp, Boulogne, Le Havre, Bordeaux, Marseille, Genoa.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: the French merchant fleet of ~700,000 tons burden in 1789 had been cut by British captures and blockade by 1805.

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld, Supplying War ch. 2: requisition let corps march on separate roads without fixed lines; Boulogne to the Danube (~700 km) in five weeks with minimal magazines.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: France had roughly 3M horses around 1800-1812 plus oxen; the army used ~100,000 horses in 1805.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: familiar terrain, Vauban fortress belt, strong popular support for national defence; no harsh-climate depth.

notes: Snapshot = French Empire at the outbreak of the War of the Third Coalition (Aug-Sep 1805), standing forces before the Ulm campaign. Population and forces count the departments of France in 1805 including the annexed Belgian, Rhenish, Piedmontese and Ligurian departments (they were France, not colonies, and supplied conscripts); the world_1800 polygon covers old France only, so it understates the territory. Vassal and allied states (Kingdom of Italy, Batavian Republic, Bavaria, Spain) are excluded and includes is empty. Grande Armee strength for the Ulm campaign: 165,200 (Clodfelter 2017 p. 152) to 210,000-235,000 (Chandler, Campaigns of Napoleon p. 384), via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulm_campaign as pointer. No COW data before 1816. Force counts by branch are reconstructions from regimental counts, grade C.

name: French Republic

areaKm2.note: world_1938 France polygon = 550,890 km2 computed on the sphere; metropolitan France ~551,500 km2.

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1939 = 41,900k (metropolitan France). HYDE/Gapminder (OWID) gives 40.3M; low spans it.

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) urban share France 1940 = 53.2%. Low = COW upop/tpop 1939 = 6,397/41,900 = 0.15 (cities over 100,000 only).

activePersonnel.note: Armed forces 5,000,000 after mobilisation (Dear & Foot p. 316, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France), minus ~0.5M in North Africa, the Levant and other colonies and ~0.15M colonial-recruited soldiers serving in France (excluded, see notes). COW milper 1940 = 5,000k agrees with the total.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: after general mobilisation most trained reservists were already called; remainder = affectes speciaux in war industry and older classes.

supportPersonnel.note: Everything outside the P roles: artillery and tank crews, engineers, signals, train, regional depots and interior, Armee de l'Air (~0.1M) and Marine (~0.16M).

count.note: Chasseurs alpins and pyreneens of the Armee des Alpes and mountain divisions; educated count.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: specialist mountain kit

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: held the Alpine front against Italy in June 1940

count.note: Horse elements of the 5 Divisions Legeres de Cavalerie and 3 spahi/cavalry brigades plus horsed squadrons of the GRDI reconnaissance groups. Educated reconstruction.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: horse cavalry in a mechanised war

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: active cavalry regiments

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: little ground-support doctrine

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional long-service navy

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: very fast large destroyers

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional navy

count.note: ~77 submarines in service Sep 1939 (Conway's).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: large but mechanically mediocre boats

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: professional crews

count.note: Batteries. Educated guess: French AA was notoriously weak in 1940 (Harvey 1990), mostly 75 mm guns of WWI design and too few 25 mm Hotchkiss.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: obsolescent guns, little fire control

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: reservist crews

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: competent but methodical staff; Gamelin's Dyle-Breda plan left no strategic reserve; slow telephone/courier command (May, Strange Victory; Doughty)

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5 (national conscript army). Evidence: many units fought hard (Gembloux, Stonne, Lille) while some reserve divisions broke at Sedan

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.25-0.5. Evidence: eight months of drole de guerre, political division, memory of 1914-18 losses

weapons.note: Anchor: between 7 (1905) and 8 (1943). Evidence: Char B1 bis 75+47 mm, 25 and 47 mm AT guns; infantry weapons partly WWI

armor.note: Anchor: 8 (rolled homogeneous armour, 1943). Evidence: cast and rolled armour 40-60 mm on S35 and B1 bis, thicker than German tanks of 1940

ships.note: Anchor: between 7 and 8. Evidence: modern fast fleet, a carrier (Bearn, obsolete), no radar

fortification.note: Anchor: 8 (concrete lines: Maginot is the anchor). Evidence: Maginot Line

logistics.note: Anchor: between 7 (railways) and 8 (motor transport). Evidence: about 300,000 army vehicles vs 120,000 German (Frieser p. 29), but rail-based methodical supply

communications.note: Anchor: between 7 (telegraph, telephone) and 8 (radio at company level). Evidence: command relied on telephone and dispatch riders; few tanks had radios

isr.note: Anchor: ISR 7 = aerial recon, 8 = radar. Evidence: aerial reconnaissance spotted the Ardennes columns but warnings were discounted; little radar

air.note: Anchor: air 7 = 1914, 8 = 1943. Evidence: D.520 and Hawk 75 modern but few; most bombers obsolete

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: COW milex 1938 = 919,284 (thousand current US$), 1939 = 1,023,651; against French national income of roughly US$10-12bn this is ~8% in 1938. Grade C (GDP conversion approximate).

industrialShare.note: Analogue: industry ~35% of French output in the late 1930s, agriculture ~25% of output with ~35% of labour. Grade C.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: France was close to self-sufficient in food in 1939, with North African imports.

annualCohort.note: Males reaching 20 in 1939-40 come from the WWI "hollow classes": French births ~0.40M in 1919 and ~0.83M in 1920, halved for males. Educated reconstruction.

armor.note: Educated guess: French tank output reached ~100-150 per month by spring 1940.

aircraft_fighter.note: Educated guess: deliveries rose sharply in spring 1940 (Hooton 2007 p. 81 reserve of ~2,000 by June); MS.406 1,077 and MB.151/152 636 built in total.

aircraft_strike.note: Educated guess: LeO 451, Breguet 691/693 and Amiot 351 in small series.

ships_major.note: Richelieu and Jean Bart completing, La Galissonniere-class cruisers completed 1936-37. Educated per-year rate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: ~80,000 km routes nationales plus ~250,000 km departmental roads; the much larger network of chemins vicinaux excluded.

railKm.note: SNCF main network ~42,600 km at its 1938 creation; high adds local and secondary lines. Grade C.

majorPorts.note: Marseille, Le Havre, Cherbourg, Brest, Toulon, Bordeaux, Saint-Nazaire, Nantes, Dunkirk, Lorient, Rouen, Calais, La Pallice.

merchantTonnage.note: Lloyd's Register 1939-40: France 1,231 steamers and motorships, 2,933,933 gross tons. Converted to deadweight at x1.5 (x1.3-1.6).

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: methodical, rail-based supply doctrine; better motorised than the Germans but organised for positional war.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~2.7M horses in France in the late 1930s; the army requisitioned ~0.5M.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: familiar terrain, Maginot Line and fortified cities, population support; no climate depth.

notes: Order of battle = 10 May 1940 (start of the Western campaign); demographic and economic values are 1939. Add them via a colonial snapshot if a scenario needs them. Army and air figures come via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France as pointer to Frieser (Blitzkrieg Legend, pp. 29, 35-37), Dear & Foot (p. 316), Hooton (2007 p. 47) and Harvey (1990). Sep 1939 differences: 98 divisions mobilised for the Saar offensive with ~2,500 tanks (same article). Navy counts are from Conway's (not fetched, grade B).

name: German Reich

areaKm2.note: world_1938 Germany polygon (already includes Austria and the Sudetenland) = ~560,000 km2 computed on the sphere; plus the Protectorate ~48,900 km2. Published Greater Germany + Protectorate 1939 is ~633,000-635,000 km2, used as mid; the polygon is low.

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1939 = 79,798k, which matches Greater Germany without the Protectorate (Altreich, Austria, Sudetenland, Memel; 1938 value 68,424k). Plus the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia ~7.4M: HYDE/Gapminder Czechia 1939 = 11.1M (OWID population CSV) minus ~3.6M ceded with the Sudetenland. Excludes the annexed Polish territories (Oct 1939).

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) urban share Germany 1940 = 53.2%, Austria 60.0%, Czechia 42%. Low = COW upop/tpop 1939 = 23,627/79,798 = 0.30 (cities over 100,000 only).

activePersonnel.note: Wehrmacht after mobilisation (26 Aug 1939): Feldheer ~2.75M, Ersatzheer ~1.0M, Luftwaffe ~0.4M, Kriegsmarine 78,000 on 1 Sep 1939 (Kriegsmarine article), SS-Verfuegungstruppe small. COW milper 1939 = 2,750k is an annual average including peacetime months, so it is not used. By May 1940 Heer 4.2M, Luftwaffe 1.0M, navy 180,000, Waffen-SS 100,000 (Frieser p. 35-37 via Battle of France article).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: conscription only from 1935, so trained reserve classes were thin; Frieser p. 29 notes half of all soldiers in 1939-40 had only weeks of training. Army grew from ~3.7M to 4.2M by May 1940.

supportPersonnel.note: Everything outside the P roles: Luftwaffe incl. flak (~0.4M), navy (78,000), artillery, panzer, engineer, signals and supply troops, staffs and the Ersatzheer.

mobilizationRatio.note: 17.3M served in Heer, Luftwaffe and navy, 18.2M with the Waffen-SS, over the whole war (Overmans 1999, via https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wehrmacht); ~13M at peak strength. Divided by ~87-90M gives ~0.15-0.21.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Infantry of ~98 infantry divisions (Poland: 66 divisions incl. reserves; West: ~43) at ~9,000-12,000 infantry each, plus fortress and frontier units. Reconstruction from division counts (Maier et al., GSWW vol. II); grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Kar98k, MG34 (best GPMG of the era), but 1st-wave divisions only fully equipped; reserve waves used Czech and WWI stocks

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: active divisions well trained; Frieser p. 29: 50% of soldiers had only weeks of training, 45% of the army over 40 by 1940

count.note: 3 Gebirgs divisions (~13,000 each) plus SS-Verfuegungstruppe regiments.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: specialist mountain equipment

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional mountain troops

count.note: 1. Kavallerie-Brigade (~6,700) plus mounted squadrons of divisional reconnaissance battalions. Educated reconstruction.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: horsed reconnaissance, obsolescent role

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: long-service cavalry cadres

count.note: Heer tank inventory 3,472, of which 2,859 with the Field Army and 408 with the Replacement Army (Jentz, Panzertruppen vol. 1 p. 88, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland); mostly Pz I and Pz II, ~300 Pz III/IV, plus Czech 35(t)/38(t).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical). Evidence: Pz I/II are machine-gun and 20 mm light tanks; but all had radios

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: panzer divisions trained in combined-arms exercises since 1935

count.note: May 1940 western force 7,378 guns (Frieser p. 35-37) is the floor; ~9,000 guns committed against Poland (Invasion of Poland infobox, pointer). Field and heavy pieces; excludes flak.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: leFH 18 and sFH 18 modern, but horse-drawn

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional artillery arm

count.note: ~1,180 fighters (Bf 109, Bf 110) on 1 Sep 1939 (Invasion of Poland article). Murray, Strategy for Defeat Table XXI: 2,916 combat aircraft actual (98.9% of authorised) in Sep 1939.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75-1.0. Evidence: Bf 109E the best fighter in service in 1939 with the Spitfire

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: Condor Legion veterans, finger-four tactics

count.note: ~1,100 bombers (He 111, Do 17, Ju 86) and 290-366 Ju 87 dive bombers (Invasion of Poland article); within Murray's 2,916 combat aircraft (Table XXI).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: modern medium bombers, Stuka precise but vulnerable

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: blind-flying and close-support training; Spain experience

count.note: Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1922-1946: Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, 3 Deutschland-class Panzerschiffe, 2 old Schlesien-class, Admiral Hipper (Bluecher commissioned 20 Sep 1939), 6 light cruisers.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: modern fast ships, Seetakt radar on some; no carrier

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: small navy, limited fleet-action practice

count.note: 21-22 destroyers (Z1-Z22) and 11-12 torpedo boats in service (Conway's 1922-1946). Minesweepers and S-boats excluded.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Z-class destroyers had unreliable high-pressure boilers

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: see above

count.note: 57 U-boats commissioned on 1 Sep 1939, ~46 operational, many Type II coastal boats.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Type VII the best attack submarine design; torpedo defects in 1939-40

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: Doenitz's intensive pre-war training

count.note: Batteries. Harvey 1990 p. 449: 2,600 88 mm and 6,700 20/37 mm guns in all German forces by May 1940; at 4 heavy or ~12 light guns per battery that is ~1,200 batteries. Sep 1939 somewhat fewer.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75-1.0. Evidence: 8.8 cm Flak 18/36 the best heavy AA gun of 1939

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: Luftwaffe flak arm, professional

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.75 (trained staff system, proven commanders). Evidence: general-staff system and Auftragstaktik; Poland won in five weeks

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75. Evidence: Wehrkreis-based regional recruitment gave unit identity; reserve divisions weaker

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: no war enthusiasm in Sep 1939 (unlike 1914); confidence rose after Poland

weapons.note: Anchor: between 7 (1905) and 8 (1943). Evidence: MG34, leFH 18, Ju 87 in service; most tanks light; 1943 types not yet

armor.note: Anchor: between 7 and 8 (rolled homogeneous armour, 1943). Evidence: Pz III/IV only ~300 of 3,472 tanks (Jentz p. 88)

ships.note: Anchor: between 7 (dreadnoughts) and 8 (carriers, radar, submarines). Evidence: modern battlecruisers, Seetakt radar, Type VII U-boats; no carrier

fortification.note: Anchor: between 7 (concrete forts) and 8 (Maginot). Evidence: Westwall bunkers, lighter than the Maginot Line

logistics.note: Anchor: between 7 (railways) and 8 (motor transport). Evidence: only ~10% of the army motorised, 120,000 vehicles vs 300,000 French; horse-drawn supply (Frieser p. 29)

communications.note: Anchor: 8 (radio at company level). Evidence: radio in every tank and command vehicle; Enigma for higher echelons

isr.note: Anchor: ISR 7 = aerial recon, 8 = radar. Evidence: Hs 126 / Do 17 reconnaissance; Freya early-warning radar in service

air.note: Anchor: air 7 = 1914, 8 = 1943. Evidence: Bf 109E, He 111, Ju 87, Ju 88 entering service

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison 2023 (OWID CSV): Germany 1939 = 8,617, Austria 1939 = 6,529, Czechoslovakia 1937 = 4,594 (2011 int$). Population-weighted Greater Germany + Protectorate ~8,000.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: COW milex 1938 = 7,415,163 (thousand current US$) and 1939 = 12,000,000; against German GNP of ~RM 100-130bn (~US$40-52bn at 2.49 RM/$) that is ~15-19% in 1938 and ~23% in 1939. Tooze (Wages of Destruction ch. 7-9) gives ~17-20% for 1938-39.

industrialShare.note: Industry and crafts roughly 45% of output in the late-1930s Reich (Tooze, Wages of Destruction ch. 4, economy overview). Grade C.

foodSurplus.note: Germany ~83% self-sufficient in food in 1939 (Tooze ch. 6, Backe's food ministry); surplus above producers' subsistence low. Educated guess.

annualCohort.note: Males reaching 19-20 in 1939: the 1919-20 birth cohorts (~1.26M and ~1.6M births in the Reich, WWI dip) halved for males, minus mortality, plus Austria and the Czech lands.

armor.note: Tanks per year: 1940 = 1,643, 1941 = 3,790 (plus ~500 assault guns) as commonly cited from Harrison/Overy; 1944 peak ~19,000 AFVs is outside the 1939 snapshot. Grade C (from memory of the tables).

aircraft_fighter.note: Murray, Strategy for Defeat Table XX: fighters 1939 = 1,856, 1940 = 3,106, 1941 = 3,732.

submarines.note: U-boats commissioned per year: ~50 in 1940, ~200 in 1941 (Conway's). Grade C.

ships_major.note: Bismarck, Tirpitz, Prinz Eugen, Bluecher completed 1939-41. Educated per-year rate.

artillery.note: Educated guess: field and heavy guns per year 1940-41.

air_defense.note: Educated guess: new flak batteries equipped per year 1940-41.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: ~215,000 km of classified roads in the Altreich plus Austria and the Czech lands; Reichsautobahn ~3,300 km by 1939.

railKm.note: Reichsbahn ~54,000-58,000 km (Altreich) plus Austrian (~5,900 km) and Czech-lands lines; reconstruction, grade C.

majorPorts.note: Hamburg, Bremen/Bremerhaven, Wilhelmshaven, Kiel, Luebeck, Stettin, Koenigsberg/Pillau, Emden, Swinemuende.

merchantTonnage.note: Lloyd's Register 1939-40: Germany 2,459 steamers and motorships, 4,482,662 gross tons. Converted to deadweight at x1.5 (x1.3-1.6) for mixed cargo fleets.

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld, Supplying War ch. 5: motor transport could sustain operations ~300-500 km beyond railheads in 1939-41; the infantry mass depended on horses and rail.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~3.4M horses in the Altreich plus Austria and the Czech lands; the army mobilised ~0.5-0.6M horses and remained largely horse-drawn (Frieser p. 29).

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: familiar terrain, Westwall and fortified cities, population support; no climate depth.

notes: Snapshot date 1 September 1939 (invasion of Poland). Territory and population = Greater Germany (Altreich incl. Saar, Austria annexed March 1938, Sudetenland Oct 1938, Memel March 1939) plus the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia (March 1939). The hb:1938:Germany polygon contains Austria and the Sudetenland but not the Protectorate. includes is empty: Austria and the Czech lands are not separate nations in 1939, so they are folded in rather than listed. Annexed Polish lands (Oct 1939) and Slovakia (client state) excluded. May 1940 reference figures for the battle agent (Frieser, Blitzkrieg Legend p. 35-37 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France): Heer 4.2M, Luftwaffe 1.0M, navy 180,000, Waffen-SS 100,000; 3.0M men in 135 divisions for the offensive; 2,439 tanks and 7,378 guns in the west; Murray Table XII: 4,782 aircraft on 11 May 1940 (1,356 single-engine fighters, 354 twin-engine, 1,711 bombers, 414 dive bombers). COW NMC v6 was not downloadable from correlatesofwar.org; v7 (2025 release) was used. Not sourced line by line: Wehrmacht total on 1 Sep 1939 (no fetched page; cited to Dear & Foot and widely reported ~4.5M).

name: Kingdom of Italy

areaKm2.note: LoN Year-Book 1938/39 Table 2: Italy 310 thousand km2. The world_1938 'Italy' feature (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_1938.geojson) computes to ~306,500 km2 (low); a second 'Italy' feature is the Dodecanese (~1,950 km2 on the polygon, ~2,700 km2 actual), included in high only.

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1940 = 44,470k (1941 = 44,830k, high). LoN Year-Book 1938/39 Table 2: 43,509k present population March 1939; 43.8M quoted for 1940 in the cited Italian military history page (low). Metropolitan Italy incl. Sicily, Sardinia, Zara and Fiume; colonies, Albania and the Dodecanese population excluded.

urbanization.note: HYDE via OWID: Italy 1940 = 49.6% urban (high; HYDE counts large agro-towns as urban). Mid 0.45 discounts this. Low = COW upop/tpop 1940 = 8,304/44,470 = 0.187 (cities over 100,000).

activePersonnel.note: Harrison 1998 Table 1-5 (Zamagni): Italian armed forces 2,340k average for 1940 (high, includes the post-June mobilisation); COW NMC v7 milper 1940 = 1,634k (low). trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: universal conscription since unification left many trained classes; strength rose from 2,340k (1940 average) to 3,227k (1941) per Harrison Table 1-5, but equipment, not men, was the limit. supportPersonnel.note: active minus P roles: navy (~170k), air force (~100k), artillery, engineers, Guardia alla Frontiera fortress troops, services and depots.

name: Kingdom of Macedon (Alexander III)

areaKm2.note: Educated guess. Analogue: the modern Greek region of Macedonia (~34,000 km2) plus Upper Macedonia/Paeonia; high adds directly ruled parts of Thrace. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/506) codes only 10,000 km2 for 359 BCE, the core before Philip II's expansion.

activePersonnel.note: Field and home armies (50,600) + League fleet crews and engineers (34,000) + margin. About half are non-Macedonians: League allies (7,000 infantry, 600 cavalry, the fleet), Greek mercenaries (5,000) and Balkan contingents (7,000+).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: Macedonians trained under Philip but not under arms; reinforcements of a few thousand were sent to Asia in 333.

supportPersonnel.note: League fleet 160 triremes x ~200 crew = 32,000 (largely allied Greeks) + ~2,000 engineers, surveyors (bematists), staff.

Line = Macedonian phalanx and hypaspists (12,000) + League hoplites (7,000) + mercenary hoplites (5,000) + Antipater's 12,000.

name: Mongol Empire

areaKm2.note: No single 1241 polygon exists. Computed on the sphere from world_1279 polygons: Great Khanate 10.49M (minus Song China ~2-2.5M and Dali, not yet conquered), Golden Horde 5.25M, Chagatai Khanate 3.32M, plus ~2M of the Ilkhanate (northern Iran, Caucasus).

population.note: Educated guess, no modern estimate for the empire at 1241 found. Built from HYDE/Gapminder country series (OWID) for 1200-1300: Mongolia 0.8M, Kazakhstan 0.96M, Uzbekistan 1.04M, Turkmenistan 0.19M, Iran 5.0M (1200, ~half under Mongol rule by 1241), China 103M (1200, of which the former Jin/Xi Xia north after the 1211-34 wars plausibly 20-30M; the 1236 Mongol census registered far fewer households). Adds Uyghur, Qipchaq steppe and Volga Bulgar lands ~2-3M. Excludes tributary vassals (Rus principalities ~6M, Georgia/Armenia, Goryeo) and Song China. (context page: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true)

urbanization.note: Analogue: HYDE urban share for China 1500 = 6.5% (OWID urbanization-last-500-years); steppe near 0, Transoxiana oases higher. Educated guess.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. Anchors: Chinggis Khan left ~129,000 men at his death in 1227 (Rashid al-Din, accepted as order of magnitude by May, Mongol Art of War ch. 2, and Morgan); by 1241 the army had absorbed Turkic (Qipchaq) contingents and Han/Khitan/Jurchen armies in North China. Field forces at once: Batu's western army (40,000-150,000), the Chinese front, Chormaqan/Baiju in Iran and the Caucasus, garrisons.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: adult nomad males outside active tumens (all trained by lifelong riding and the nerge hunt, May ch. 2) plus subject levies callable within a month.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess: Chinese and Muslim siege engineers, artisans, yam relay staff and baggage handlers attached to the armies (May ch. 4 on siege specialists).

mobilizationRatio.note: Mongol nomads mobilised nearly every adult male (decimal levy, ~1 soldier per 4-5 people of the nomadic population, cf. May, Mongol Art of War ch. 2), but the sedentary majority supplied only levies and auxiliaries. Applied to the whole subject population this gives a few percent. Educated guess.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Horse archers, the majority of every tumen (May ch. 3 puts light horse at roughly 60% of a Mongol army). Share of the active-force guess; western army alone 40,000 (Rashid al-Din via Sverdrup 2010 p. 115) to 120,000-150,000 (older modern estimates), see notes.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75-1.0 (among the era's best). Evidence: composite bow outranging European crossbows in the field; 3-5 remounts per man (May ch. 3)

training.note: Rubric row: training 1.0 (elite long-service). Evidence: lifelong riders, decimal units drilled by the nerge battue hunt (May ch. 2)

count.note: Lancers in lamellar armour, roughly 40% of tumens per May ch. 3 (disputed; some put it nearer 30%). Educated split of the active-force guess.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75 (among the era's best) minus. Evidence: lamellar and leather-iron armour lighter than Latin knights' mail; horses smaller

training.note: Rubric row: training 1.0. Evidence: same decimal system and campaign experience as the light horse

count.note: Han, Khitan and Jurchen foot in North China under Mongol command (May ch. 4 on incorporated sedentary troops). Educated guess.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical). Evidence: Jin-era equipment

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: mix of ex-Jin regulars and levies

count.note: Chinese crossbowmen and siege archers attached to the North China armies. Educated guess.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Chinese crossbows, era-typical to good

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: levies and ex-Jin regulars

count.note: Siege engines (traction and counterweight trebuchets, ballistae) built on site by Chinese and Muslim engineers (May ch. 4). At the Sajo bridge (Mohi 1241) the Mongols used seven stone throwers (Wikipedia pointer to Sverdrup/Jackson). Empire-wide count is an educated guess.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75 (among the era's best). Evidence: Chinese and Persian siege technology, best available in Eurasia

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: specialist engineer corps (May ch. 4)

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 1.0 (best-in-era: "Mongols 1241" is the rubric example). Evidence: Subotai and Batu coordinated five columns across Poland and Hungary, winning Legnica and Mohi within two days (Jackson, Mongols and the West ch. 3)

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75-1.0. Evidence: decimal units with collective responsibility; tumens mixed Mongol cores with Turkic recruits (May ch. 2)

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75 (motivated, recent victories). Evidence: unbroken run of victories 1219-1240 (Khwarazm, Jin, Rus)

weapons.note: Anchor: 4 (1250: crossbow, trebuchet). Evidence: composite bow, Chinese crossbows, counterweight trebuchets and incendiaries in the siege train (May ch. 4)

armor.note: Anchor: between 3 (mail) and 4 (plate-and-mail). Evidence: lamellar of iron and lacquered leather, lighter than contemporary Latin armour

ships.note: Anchor: 1 (oared riverboats). Evidence: no navy in 1241; river craft captured from the Jin. Naval warfare only under the later Yuan

fortification.note: Anchor: between 3 (ashlar walls, siege towers) and 4. Evidence: held walled Jin and Khwarazmian cities but built little; Karakorum walled c. 1235

logistics.note: Anchor: 4 (1250: river transport, granaries). Evidence: self-moving herds and remounts gave unmatched operational reach on grassland (May ch. 4)

communications.note: Anchor: 4 is defined by the yam relay itself. Evidence: the yam relay network founded under Ogedei (1234) was the era's best; arrow and flag signals in battle

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years: 1250 -> 4. Evidence: deep cavalry screens and spies; intelligence on Hungary gathered years before 1241 (Jackson ch. 3)

gdpPerCapita.note: Analogue: Maddison 2023 China 1090 = 1,222 and 1150 = 1,181 (2011 int$, via OWID grapher CSV). Scaled down for the war-ravaged north and the large pastoral share (steppe output per head assumed well below the Chinese level). Educated guess, grade D.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$. Grade D inputs.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. The nomadic core was an army; tribute from sedentary subjects largely fed it. No documented budget.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: crafts in North China and Transoxiana cities, much reduced by the conquest; pastoral and farm output dominant.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: pastoral herds fed the army on the march; North China agriculture disrupted by the 1211-34 wars.

annualCohort.note: Educated guess. Low = 15-year-old males of the ~1.5-2M nomadic Mongol-Turkic population that fed the tumens; high = all males reaching 15 across the 36M subjects (~1.1%/yr x 1/2).

roadKm.note: Educated guess: engineered roads only in former Jin North China and Khwarazmian oases; steppe movement was cross-country along yam routes.

majorPorts.note: No sea-going fleet or naval port in 1241; Jin river harbours only.

merchantTonnage.note: No Mongol merchant marine in 1241 (maritime trade came with the Yuan after 1279). Educated guess.

supplyRangeKm.note: Herds and remounts let armies operate far from base where pasture existed (May ch. 4); the western army campaigned >3,000 km from Mongolia but on steppe pasture, and pasture limits in Hungary are one argument for the 1242 withdrawal. Educated guess for range beyond a base.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: Mongolia carries ~4M horses for ~3M people today; 13th-c. nomads kept 3-5 remounts per warrior plus oxen and camels; Qipchaq steppe and North China added more.

homeDefense.note: 1.3 row for the Mongolian homeland (deep steppe depth, harsh continental climate invaders are not adapted to); conquered sedentary lands give little home advantage, so mid 1.25.

notes: Border: hb:1279:Great Khanate chosen over hb:1200:Mongol Empire. The 1200 polygon (5.4M km2) is the pre-1206 Mongol homeland only and misses North China, Central Asia and the western steppe; 1279 is also the closer file in years (38 vs 41). The Great Khanate polygon holds Karakorum, Mongolia and North China but wrongly includes Song South China and Dali (conquered 1253-79) and omits the western ulus (Golden Horde polygon) from which the 1241 invasion came. A union of world_1279 features with SUBJECTO = "Mongol Empire" minus Song and Tibet would be the honest border. Army sizes are the weakest part. Western (Batu/Subotai) army: Rashid al-Din gives ~40,000 horsemen for the 1241 invasion of Central Europe, read by Sverdrup (J. Medieval Military History 8, 2010, p. 115) as a nominal force of at least 30,000; Khrustalev puts the 1237-40 Rus campaign at ~60,000; older modern estimates run 120,000-150,000 (all via the Battle of Mohi and Kievan Rus' invasion articles as pointers, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mohi). Medieval chroniclers' 200,000-500,000 are rejected. Empire-wide totals are educated guesses. Population convention: directly ruled lands only; tributary Rus principalities, Georgia, Armenia and Goryeo excluded (includes is empty). All ratings use the rubric in data/SOURCES.md.

name: Achaemenid Empire (Xerxes I)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 4.8-5.5 million km2 for 500-451 BCE. The historical-basemaps world_bc500 polygon measures 5.95 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, high).

population.note: Seshat codes 20-26 million for 500 BCE (mid = 23 million) and 17-35 million for 400 BCE (range). Everything inside the 480 BCE imperial border incl. Egypt, Babylonia, Ionia, Bactria and the Indus satrapy.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat codes the largest settlement at 200,000 (Babylon). Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Levant and Ionia were urbanised; the Iranian plateau and Central Asia much less. Scaled below the Roman 10-25% (Hanson & Ortman 2017).

activePersonnel.note: Invasion land army (80,000 / 152,000 / 300,000) + fleet crews (102,000 / 150,000 / 241,000, see supportPersonnel) + garrisons across the empire left behind (40,000 / 60,000 / 100,000; educated guess: Elephantine, Babylon, Sardis, satrapal guards). Garrisons are not broken down by role in `forces`.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: Iranian and satrapal cavalry and levies reachable within ~30 days; the empire's distances make most levies slower than that.

supportPersonnel.note: Fleet crews: triremes (600 / 750 / 1,207) x ~170-200 men (oarsmen, deck crew, the ~30 marines per ship that Herodotus mentions). Excludes the transport crews.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess for an agrarian empire levying satrapal contingents (hatru land-for-service system): the 480 expedition plus fleet (~300,000 men) was already ~1.3% of the population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Land army of the 480 invasion: low 80,000 (Shahbazi 2012, Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, p. 129: 80,000-100,000 or fewer), mid 150,000, high 300,000 (Munro and Macan, from six marshals and 29 myriarchs). Herodotus 7.60-99 gives 1,700,000 infantry and 80,000 cavalry (rejected). Split by role on the composition in Herodotus' muster list (Iranian archer infantry dominant): Iranian and Saka archer infantry incl. the 10,000 Immortals (Herodotus 7.83) ~46%.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5 era-typical: composite bows, wicker shields (spara), little armour.

training.note: Immortals professional (0.75); most contingents satrapal levies (0.25-0.5).

count.note: Land army of the 480 invasion: low 80,000 (Shahbazi 2012, Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, p. 129: 80,000-100,000 or fewer), mid 150,000, high 300,000 (Munro and Macan, from six marshals and 29 myriarchs). Herodotus 7.60-99 gives 1,700,000 infantry and 80,000 cavalry (rejected). Split by role on the composition in Herodotus' muster list (Iranian archer infantry dominant): spear-armed close-order contingents (Assyrians, Egyptians, Anatolians, Ionian hoplites) ~26%.

quality.note: Below the Greek hoplite panoply; between obsolete and era-typical.

training.note: Mostly levies (rubric 0.25-0.5).

count.note: Land army of the 480 invasion: low 80,000 (Shahbazi 2012, Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, p. 129: 80,000-100,000 or fewer), mid 150,000, high 300,000 (Munro and Macan, from six marshals and 29 myriarchs). Herodotus 7.60-99 gives 1,700,000 infantry and 80,000 cavalry (rejected). Split by role on the composition in Herodotus' muster list (Iranian archer infantry dominant): javelin and other light levies (Thracians, Libyans, Ethiopians, Arabians) ~17%.

quality.note: Light, often traditional equipment (rubric 0.25).

training.note: Levies (rubric 0.25).

count.note: Land army of the 480 invasion: low 80,000 (Shahbazi 2012, Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, p. 129: 80,000-100,000 or fewer), mid 150,000, high 300,000 (Munro and Macan, from six marshals and 29 myriarchs). Herodotus 7.60-99 gives 1,700,000 infantry and 80,000 cavalry (rejected). Split by role on the composition in Herodotus' muster list (Iranian archer infantry dominant): the two 1,000-strong Persian guard cavalry regiments (Herodotus 7.40-41) and armoured noble cavalry ~1.3%.

quality.note: Armoured noble cavalry; era-typical to good.

training.note: Royal guard professionals (rubric 0.75).

count.note: Land army of the 480 invasion: low 80,000 (Shahbazi 2012, Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, p. 129: 80,000-100,000 or fewer), mid 150,000, high 300,000 (Munro and Macan, from six marshals and 29 myriarchs). Herodotus 7.60-99 gives 1,700,000 infantry and 80,000 cavalry (rejected). Split by role on the composition in Herodotus' muster list (Iranian archer infantry dominant): Iranian and Saka horse archers and javelin cavalry ~10%.

quality.note: Mounted archers/javelinmen, era-typical.

training.note: Iranian nobility and steppe horsemen, raised in the saddle.

count.note: Lazenby 1993 (The Defence of Greece, p. 93 per citation key) argues for no more than ~600 warships; Shahbazi 2012 gives 600-1,200; Herodotus 7.89 gives 1,207 triremes (Phoenicia 300, Egypt 200, Cyprus 150...). Mid 750 between them. ~3,000 transports/penteconters (Herodotus) not counted as combatants.

quality.note: Phoenician triremes among the era's best (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Professional Phoenician and Ionian seafarers.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5: competent staff (outstanding logistics planning: canal at Athos, Hellespont bridges, depots), average generalship in battle.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: multi-ethnic host of ~46 contingents with separate languages; core Persian units better.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5 average; royal presence raised it, subject levies low.

weapons.note: Between anchor 2 (composite bow, bronze) and 3 (iron weapons, torsion artillery): iron weapons common, no torsion artillery yet.

armor.note: Anchor 2 (bronze scale) to 3: scale and linen armour for elites, most infantry unarmoured.

ships.note: Anchor 3 triremes (Phoenician), no larger polyremes yet.

fortification.note: Anchor 2-3: stone citadels, Babylon's walls; Seshat codes a 60 km long wall.

logistics.note: Anchor 3: Royal Road and depot system documented in the Persepolis Fortification tablets (Briant, isbn:1575060310, ch. 9).

communications.note: Anchor 3: mounted relay posts (angareion) on the royal roads.

isr.note: Year anchor (480 BCE between 2 and 3): mounted scouts, spies.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: year 1 CE values for Iran, Iraq, Egypt, Israel and Jordan are 1,116, Turkey 897 (2011 int$). Applied 500 years earlier to the same region; Central Asian and Indian satrapies probably lower, hence mid 1,000.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Herodotus 3.89-95 lists ~14,560 Euboic talents of annual tribute, not convertible to GDP reliably; most military service was paid in land grants (hatru).

industrialShare.note: Educated guess for an agrarian empire with craft centres in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Lydia.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: irrigated Mesopotamian and Egyptian agriculture produced large surpluses stored in royal granaries (Persepolis tablets).

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical snapshots.

roadKm.note: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander, ch. 9: the Sardis-Susa Royal Road (Herodotus 5.52-53: 450 parasangs, ~2,500 km) is the low bound; the Persepolis tablets attest further routes to Persepolis, Ecbatana, Bactra, Arachosia and Egypt. Total length not documented; mid and high are educated guesses.

majorPorts.note: Phoenicia (Sidon, Tyre, Arwad, Byblos), Cyprus (Salamis), Cilicia, Egypt, Ionia and the Hellespont; count of ports able to supply a fleet is an estimate.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Herodotus' ~3,000 transports and penteconters x ~50 t.

supplyRangeKm.note: The 480 army advanced along the coast with the fleet and pre-stocked depots on the Thracian coast (Herodotus 7.25); away from the sea and depots its range was short.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.07-0.11 draft and pack animals (incl. camels) per inhabitant x population.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2 (local supply, fortified cities); deep strategic depth and desert climate argue for 1.3, weak loyalty of subject peoples for less.

notes: Snapshot = spring 480 BCE, Xerxes' invasion of Greece; forces are the expeditionary army and fleet at campaign start, garrisons elsewhere only in activePersonnel. Herodotus' figures (2,641,610 men, 1,207 triremes) are not used as mid values; modern estimates range from under 100,000 to ~300,000 for the land army. Macedon and Thrace were tributary in 480 but are not inside the bc500 polygon and are not counted. Population convention: inside the border, Seshat range.

name: Roman Empire (Trajan)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 5.8 million km2 for 100 CE (high). Taagepera 1979 (doi:10.2307/1170959, not fetched) gives ~5.0 million km2 at the 117 CE peak (mid). The historical-basemaps world_100 polygon measures 4.62 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, low); it predates Trajan's eastern annexations of 114-117.

population.note: Seshat codes the Principate at 50-60 million for 100 CE and 55-70 million for 200 CE. Frier 2000 (Cambridge Ancient History XI, isbn:0521263352, p. 814 table 6) gives 45.5 million in 14 CE and 61.4 million in 164 CE; geometric interpolation to 117 CE gives ~56 million, used as mid. High end covers Scheidel's 59-72 million for c. 165 CE and the 70 million upper Seshat value. Everything inside the imperial border, slaves included.

urbanization.note: Hanson & Ortman 2017 (JRA 30, pp. 301-324) put ~14 million people in ~600 cities above 5,000 inhabitants, i.e. 20-25% of a 56-70 million population (high end). Mid and low allow for stricter urban definitions; Seshat codes Rome itself at 1.0-1.2 million in 100 CE.

activePersonnel.note: Holder 2003 (BICS 46, 101-145) reconstructs the army of c. 130 CE as 30 legions (165,000 infantry + 3,600 cavalry) and 381 auxiliary units (152,260 infantry + 71,468 cavalry) = 392,328, excluding ~4,000 officers. Added: Praetorian and urban cohorts (~10,000-20,000), numeri (~5,000-20,000) and the navy (30,000-46,000). Trajan in 117 also had 30 legions (II Traiana and XXX Ulpia raised, IX Hispana and XXII Deiotariana still extant). Vigiles (~7,000) excluded as paramilitary.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. No formal reserve; recalled veterans (evocati) and recently discharged veterans in colonies. 30 legions x ~150-200 survivors of 25-year service discharged per year = ~5,000-6,000 legionaries a year; a few recent year classes recallable.

supportPersonnel.note: Navy 30,000-46,000 (John Lydus gives 45,562 sailors for the fleet before Diocletian's expansion; ancient figure, late) + ~4,000 centurions and higher officers excluded from Holder's unit totals (Holder 2003, doi:10.1111/j.2041-5370.2003.tb01979.x). Mid = 40,000 navy + 4,000 officers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The standing army was ~0.8% of the population; the Republic during the Second Punic War mobilised a far larger share of its citizen body, but provincials could not be levied at that intensity. 0.04 assumes an emergency levy on the Republican pattern restricted to citizen and frontier populations.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Legionary infantry 30 x ~5,500 = 165,000 + auxiliary infantry 152,260 less ~12,000 archers (Holder 2003, as tabulated for c. 130 CE) + Praetorian and urban cohorts in Rome (~10,000-20,000, estimate). Auxiliary cohorts fought as close-order armoured infantry, hence line.

quality.note: Rubric quality 1.0 row names Roman legion kit c. 100 CE as the era's best (mail/segmented armour, scutum, gladius, pilum); auxiliaries slightly lighter, so mid 0.95.

training.note: Rubric training 0.75-1.0: long-service professionals (25-year terms), drill and fortified-camp routine; auxiliaries slightly below legionaries.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (300 BCE: iron weapons, torsion artillery) plus refinements (pilum, gladius, carroballista); SOURCES.md names Rome 117 CE weapons ~3.3.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (iron cuirass, mail) exceeded: segmented plate and mail standard issue; well short of anchor 4 plate-and-mail.

ships.note: Anchor 3: triremes, liburnians, a few larger polyremes.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 (ashlar walls, siege towers) plus permanent stone legionary fortresses and a fortified limes.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 (engineered roads, depots) plus empire-wide granaries, annona shipping and river transport (part of anchor 4).

isr.note: Year anchor 3: exploratores, speculatores, frontier watchtowers.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 (2011 int$) values for year 1 CE in Roman territory: Italy 1,407, Greece 1,275, Egypt/Levant/Tunisia 1,116, France/Belgium/Portugal 956, Turkey 897, Spain 886. Mid ~1,000 is the rough population-weighted provincial average (Italy is ~1/8 of the population). Cross-check: Scheidel & Friesen 2009 (doi:10.3815/007543509789745223) put output at ~1.7-1.9x bare subsistence, consistent with this range.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Duncan-Jones, Money and Government in the Roman Empire (1994), ch. 3: army cost ~600-650 million HS a year in the 2nd century; GDP ~18 billion HS (Scheidel & Friesen 2009, doi:10.3815/007543509789745223: ~260 HS per head) -> ~3.5%.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess for an agrarian economy where ~75-85% of output was agricultural; mining, textiles, ceramics and construction make up the rest.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: GDP ~1.7-1.9x bare-bones subsistence (Scheidel & Friesen 2009) implies a modest surplus that fed ~15-20% urban population and the army.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical snapshots.

roadKm.note: ORBIS v1 (Scheidel & Meeks 2012) models 84,631 km of principal roads and desert tracks c. 200 CE; it reproduces arterial routes only, so the full engineered network was larger (high).

majorPorts.note: ORBIS has 268 sea-port sites; ports able to supply a fleet or army (Ostia/Portus, Puteoli, Misenum, Ravenna, Alexandria, Carthage, Seleucia Pieria, Caesarea, Ephesus, Corinth, Massilia, Aquileia, Byzantium, Gades, Londinium...) estimated at ~20.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Rome alone imported ~200,000-300,000 t of grain a year; at ~2 voyages a season that needs ~100,000-150,000 t of shipping, and the annona was perhaps a quarter to a third of seaborne trade.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying their own grain and pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water; the Roman soldier carried ~3 days' rations plus mule-borne reserves.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.05-0.11 draft and pack animals (oxen, mules, donkeys, horses, camels) per inhabitant x population.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: familiar terrain and local supply plus fortified cities, the limes and broad population support; not 1.3 because the core is not protected by harsh climate.

notes: Snapshot = August 117 CE, at Trajan's death, the territorial peak. Population convention: everything inside the imperial border, slaves included; Armenia and Mesopotamia (annexed 114-116, abandoned by Hadrian in 118) are inside the border but their population is not counted in the mid. Border uses historical-basemaps world_100 (closest file), which shows the empire before the eastern annexations. Force numbers are Holder's c. 130 CE reconstruction (published unit lists, Hadrianic) applied to 117; the totals at Trajan's death were within a few percent (same number of legions). Navy numbers and ship counts are weak (no surviving order of battle). GDP per capita from the Maddison Project year-1 values for Roman provinces; all ancient GDP figures are reconstructions.

name: Sparta (Lakedaimon)
